title: Botanical and Horticultural Records
conventions: Every entry has a 'type'. 'worked': a plant worked with, numbered 001, 002… 'studied': a species investigated but not worked with, numbered S001, S002… 'event': a lecture, visit, course or other attendance, numbered E001, E002… 'day': a day worked at a site, as a volunteer, on contract or on an own project, numbered D001, D002… Each type has its own sequence. A work day is linked to the plants worked with on the same date at the same site; that link is worked out from the two entries and is not stored. A day's 'tasks' list holds work that did not involve a specific plant. null means not yet recorded. Text fields are plain text; the only markup allowed is … around botanical names. For plants, 'name' is the plain-text form of 'name_html'. Dates are ISO 8601. 'projects' is a list: an entry can belong to none, one or several, and never appears twice. 'image' is one photo per entry, or null. kind 'own' is D.C. Chambers' photograph; kind 'reference' is a photo of the species from a public source, with its credit, licence and source. An 'own' photo replaces a 'reference' one.

records.name: Eucalyptus badjensis Beuzev. & M.B.Welch
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 18 Jul 2026 — not keyed
records.habit: Tree; subtropical biome; to 45 m in habitat
records.diagnostic: Rough grey-brown bark at the base, smooth above and often shed in ribbons. Juvenile leaves sessile and lanceolate. Adult leaves linear to narrow-lanceolate, curved, dull green on both surfaces. Buds in threes in the leaf axils, oval, with a conical operculum. Fruit a small conical to bell-shaped capsule, 3–5 × 4–6 mm.
records.work_done: Planted.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 28 Sep 2026. IPNI 592709-1: J. Proc. Roy. Soc. New South Wales 58: 177 (1924). EUCLID.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic taken from secondary sources; check against the tree. Near misses unsourced.

records.name: Muehlenbeckia complexa (A.Cunn.) Meisn.
records.det: D.C. Chambers, 31 Jul 2026 — from bed label, not keyed
records.note: Label: the common name belongs to M. axillaris; the binomial is correct.
records.common_names: Wire vine, maidenhair vine, mattress vine, scrambling pōhuehue
records.native_range: Lord Howe Is. to New Zealand
records.diagnostic: Wiry red-brown stems, densely interlaced. Leaves petiolate, markedly variable in shape and size on one plant, margins entire or lobed. Flowers small, greenish-white.
records.near_misses: M. axillaris: mat-forming, leaves under 1 cm, glossy. M. astonii: shrub with heart-shaped leaves, not a scrambler.
records.work_done: Pruned hard with secateurs; the plant had overtaken the bed. THD asked for a wavy structure. First attempt; the work was finished by another volunteer.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 7 Sep 2026.
records.open_questions: Provenance. What the finisher changed, and why. Whether the wavy form is a shape THD maintains or a one-off.

records.name: Alluaudia montagnacii Rauh
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 7 Aug 2026 — not keyed
records.habit: Tree; desert or dry shrubland biome
records.diagnostic: Spiny succulent tree of about 2.4–6 m with a columnar main trunk carrying strong, upright branches. Small leaves about 1.5 cm long sit in regular rows among dense, black-tipped spines of 2–2.5 cm. Leaves drop in the dry season. Flowers small, green to yellow.
records.work_done: Cutting taken for propagation; left to callus for one week.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Adansonia, n.s., 1: 43 (1961). Wikipedia, Alluaudia montagnacii.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. Wikipedia calls it probably a natural hybrid of A. ascendens and A. procera, and gives IUCN Endangered; confirm both. Compare record 007.

records.name: Aloidendron barberae (Dyer) Klopper & Gideon F.Sm.
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 14 Aug 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Syn. Aloe bainesii Dyer; Aloe barberae Dyer (basionym).
records.habit: Succulent tree; seasonally dry tropical biome
records.diagnostic: Africa's largest aloe: a tree to about 15 m with a trunk up to 0.9 m across and smooth grey bark. Stems fork repeatedly in twos to build a rounded crown. Each branch ends in a dense rosette of long, narrow, dark green, deeply channelled, recurved leaves with toothed edges. Tubular salmon-pink flowers, green-tipped in bud, in cylindrical racemes in winter.
records.work_done: Planted, after thoroughly cleaning potential pests from the layers of foliage and roots.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Phytotaxa 76: 9 (2013). SANBI PlantZAfrica, Aloidendron barberae.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant.

records.name: Aloe arborescens Mill. var. lutea
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 14 Aug 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Name as determined. POWO does not list var. lutea, as an accepted name or as a synonym. The RHS lists the plant as Aloe arborescens yellow-flowered.
records.habit: Succulent shrub or tree; desert or dry shrubland biome
records.diagnostic: Many-headed, branching shrub of 2–3 m, each stem ending in a rosette of grey-green, sword-shaped leaves edged with conspicuous pale teeth. Flower spikes in winter, usually two or more per rosette. Normally deep orange to scarlet; the yellow form has green-tipped buds opening pale yellow and is otherwise identical.
records.work_done: Planted, after thoroughly cleaning potential pests from the layers of foliage and roots.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Gard. Dict., ed. 8: n.° 3 (1768). SANBI PlantZAfrica; RHS; Ruth Bancroft Garden.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. Ask THD where the name var. lutea comes from.

records.name: Banksia marginata Cav.
records.how_studied: Explained on site by T. Hart Dyke.
records.note: Garden label reads: Proteaceae / Banksia marginata / "Honeysuckle Banksia" / Tasmania.
records.diagnostic: Very variable, from a 20 cm heath shrub to a 12 m tree. Bark pale grey, smooth at first, finely tessellated with age. Leaves alternate, narrow, 1.5–6 cm long, dull green above and white beneath, usually with a blunt or notched tip; young leaves toothed. Pale yellow cylindrical spikes 5–10 cm tall from late summer to early winter, then small follicles.
records.near_misses: B. integrifolia: larger leaves and flowers, leaves whorled. B. canei: sharp points on the leaves, stouter spikes, larger follicles that stay closed for years.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Anales Hist. Nat. 1: 227 (1799). Trees and Shrubs Online; ClimateWatch; Wikipedia.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant.

records.name: Brachychiton rupestris (T.Mitch. ex Lindl.) K.Schum.
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 14 Aug 2026 — not keyed
records.common_names: Queensland bottle tree, narrow-leaved bottle tree
records.diagnostic: Drought-deciduous tree of 10–25 m with a swollen, bottle-shaped trunk 1–3.5 m across and dark grey, tessellated and fissured bark. Adult leaves narrow, 4–11 cm long, glossy above; juvenile leaves divided into 3–9 narrow lobes. Panicles of cream-yellow, red-marked flowers, then woody boat-shaped follicles in groups of 3–5.
records.near_misses: B. compactus (Proserpine bottle tree): more oval leaves, more compact flower heads, longer ellipsoid follicles.
records.work_done: Planted, after thoroughly cleaning potential pests from the layers of foliage and roots.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Engler & Prantl, Nat. Pflanzenfam. 3(6): 96 (1893). Wikipedia, Brachychiton rupestris.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. IPNI gives the combination as (Lindl.) K.Schum., 1890; POWO followed here.

records.name: Ceiba speciosa (A.St.-Hil., A.Juss. & Cambess.) Ravenna
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 28 Aug 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Syn. Chorisia speciosa A.St.-Hil., A.Juss. & Cambess. (basionym, 1828).
records.common_names: Silk floss tree, floss silk tree
records.native_range: Brazil to Peru and NE. Argentina
records.diagnostic: Deciduous tree that can exceed 25 m, with a bottle-shaped trunk swollen in its lower third. Trunk and branches carry stout conical prickles; bark green when young, grey with age. Leaves palmate with five to seven leaflets. Flowers 10–15 cm across, five petals, creamy-white at the centre and pink towards the tips. Woody ovoid capsules about 20 cm long hold black seeds in silky floss.
records.near_misses: C. chodatii: flowers of similar form and size, but creamy-white with yellow tips, not pink.
records.work_done: Pruned and dressed.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Onira 3: 46 (1998). Wikipedia, Ceiba speciosa.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant.

records.name: Conophytum minimum (Haw.) N.E.Br.
records.det: Woodside Cacti (nursery label), read by D.C. Chambers — not keyed
records.note: Labelled as Conophytum wittebergensis, a misspelling of C. wittebergense de Boer, which POWO treats as a synonym of C. minimum.
records.habit: Succulent subshrub; desert or dry shrubland biome
records.provenance: Bought at the Cactus at the Castle event, Lullingstone Castle, 5 Sep 2026. Label: Woodside Cacti (woodsidecacti.co.uk), £5.50.
records.diagnostic: Tiny, almost stemless, winter-growing leaf succulent to about 3 cm tall, forming dense mats in time. Bodies under 1 cm across, silvery-green, marked with dark brownish-red or purple dots and lines. Small, whitish, strongly scented flowers open at night in autumn.
records.work_done: Watered in error after buying. Reported by D.C. Chambers on 5 Oct 2026 as killed by the watering, with one plant thought still alive.
records.observed: Photograph, shared 5 Oct 2026: one body plump and grey-green with dark line markings; a second dried out and papery.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 5 Oct 2026. Gard. Chron., ser. 3, 71: 307 (1922); C. wittebergense: Succulenta (Netherlands) 44: 21 (1965). LLIFLE.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from a secondary source, written for the wittebergense form; check against the plant. How many plants were bought, and when the photograph was taken, not recorded. CITES listing not confirmed.

records.name: Nesocodon mauritianus (I.Richardson) Thulin
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 18 Sep 2026 — not keyed
records.habit: Subshrub or shrub; wet tropical biome
records.provenance: Two plants from Mike Clifford, arrived Sept 2026. One kept by T. Hart Dyke in a polytunnel; one by D.C. Chambers for a vivarium.
records.diagnostic: Dwarf, straggly shrub 30–40 cm tall with unbranched, hairless woody stems grooved by old leaf scars. records.name: Tagetes erecta L.
records.det: From D.C. Chambers' photographs of 18 Sep 2026, determined with Claude 3 Oct 2026 — not keyed, not confirmed by T. Hart Dyke
records.note: The French marigold of gardens, Tagetes patula L., which POWO treats as a synonym of T. erecta. A tall single-flowered form; cultivar not known.
records.diagnostic: Tall, loose, branching plant with reddish stems. Leaves pinnate, the leaflets narrow and toothed. Flower heads single, on long stalks swollen just below the head: about five broad yellow rays, each blotched red-brown at the base, around a small orange disc.
records.near_misses: African marigold forms of T. erecta: large, dense double heads of one colour on a stouter plant. T. tenuifolia: much finer leaves and many small flowers. Calendula officinalis: leaves simple, not divided.
records.work_done: Watered.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 3 Oct 2026. Sp. Pl.: 887 (1753).
records.open_questions: Determined from photographs only; confirm with T. Hart Dyke, and ask which cultivar or seed strain was sown.

records.location: The World Garden, South Africa bed
records.name: Chamaerops humilis L.
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 25 Sep 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Planted in the South Africa bed, though the species belongs in the North Africa bed: an executive decision for practicality and aesthetics.
records.diagnostic: Clumping fan palm: several stems from one base, suckering from an underground rhizome. Stems slow, 2–5 m, clothed in old leaf bases and fibre. Leaves stiff, rounded fans of 10–20 narrow leaflets. Leaf stalks armed with numerous sharp, needle-like spines.
records.near_misses: Trachycarpus fortunei: a single stem with no suckers at the base, and leaf stalks without spines.
records.work_done: Dug out an old rootball. Dug a significant hole and added sand for drainage. Planted a 7-foot specimen, with notable effort spent positioning and orienting it to sit well against the sculptures around it. Dressed with sand and ornamental warthogs.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 3 Oct 2026. Sp. Pl.: 1187 (1753). Wikipedia.
records.open_questions: What the old rootball dug out was. Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant.

records.location: The World Garden, North America bed
records.name: Ribes speciosum Pursh
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 1 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.label_read: “Grossulariaceae / Ribes speciosum / “Fuchsia Flowered Currant” / California, SW USA”
records.note: Label: published sources call it a gooseberry, not a currant, as it is spiny. POWO's range also takes in Baja California.
records.diagnostic: Spiny deciduous shrub to about 3 m, with bristly shoots and three long spines at each node. Leaves small (about 2–3 cm), glossy dark green, leathery, shallowly 3–5-lobed, mostly hairless. Pendulous, fuchsia-like, rich red flowers, four-parted, with red stamens projecting far beyond the flower. Berry red, covered in glandular bristles, about 1 cm long.
records.work_done: Cut right back.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Fl. Amer. Sept. 2: 731 (1813). Trees and Shrubs Online; Wikipedia.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. Four-parted flowers are unusual in the genus, which is otherwise five-parted.

records.name: Euphorbia heptagona L.
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 2 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Determined and labelled as Euphorbia enopla var. viridis A.C.White, R.A.Dyer & B.Sloane, which POWO treats as a synonym of E. heptagona.
records.diagnostic: Densely branched, spiny, dioecious succulent shrub about 30–100 cm tall, branching from the base and resembling a cactus, with white latex. Ridged stems carry lines of long stout spines, which are persistent sterile flower-stalks.
records.near_misses: Typical E. enopla: spines red, darkening with age. In var. viridis they are yellowish-green.
records.work_done: Dug out and disposed of.
records.observed: Had fallen over and was rotten.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Sp. Pl.: 450 (1753); var. viridis: Succ. Euphorb.: 964 (1941). LLIFLE; Wikipedia.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. LLIFLE still accepts E. enopla Boiss. Latex is an irritant. CITES listing not confirmed.

records.name: Cordyline banksii Hook.f. ‘Sprilecflash’
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 2 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Sold as Electric Flash, a trade name; the cultivar name is ‘Sprilecflash’ (RHS). The tag gives no species.
records.common_names: Cabbage palm; for the species: forest cabbage tree, tī ngahere
records.diagnostic: Evergreen, multi-stemmed, palm-like shrub of 1.5–2.5 m by 1–1.5 m. Long, pointed, lance-shaped leaves start erect then arch outwards; striped lengthwise, with a reddish-brown centre and creamy-yellow margins. Scented white flowers in summer.
records.near_misses: ‘Sprilecpink’ (Electric Pink), its parent: leaves red-purple and brown, without the yellow stripes.
records.work_done: Planted. Room was made for it by moving the Dyckia frigida slightly.
records.sources: RHS Horticultural Database, accessed 2 Oct 2026. POWO (species), accessed 2 Oct 2026: Gard. Chron. 1860: 792 (1860). US Plant Patent PP26,267.
records.open_questions: A whole-plant mutation of ‘Sprilecpink’, found 2008 (patent). Confirm the species with THD.

records.name: Cleome arborea
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 2 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.label_read: “Cleome arborea PW” (handwritten; PW = Plant World Seeds)
records.note: Name as supplied; POWO accepts no Cleome arborea. Probably Cleomella arborea (Nutt.) Roalson & J.C.Hall, inferred from the supplier's common names. Not confirmed.
records.native_range: If Cleomella arborea: California to Mexico (Baja California)
records.habit: If Cleomella arborea: shrub; desert or dry shrubland biome
records.provenance: Raised from seed from Plant World Seeds.
records.diagnostic: If Cleomella arborea: densely branched, finely hairy, strong-smelling shrub 0.5–2 m tall. Leaves usually of three equal, oval to elliptic, pointed leaflets 15–45 mm long. Flowers bright yellow, four petals of 8–14 mm, six stamens projecting well beyond them. Fruit an inflated leathery capsule 30–60 mm long.
records.work_done: Repotted into an air-pot for display outside the nursery. Explicitly not for sale.
records.observed: T. Hart Dyke noted that this is a rare type which flowers yellow, and that only certain visitors would notice.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026: Phytotaxa 205: 137 (2015). Plant World Seeds catalogue; Wikipedia.
records.open_questions: Confirm the identity against the plant: three leaflets, yellow flowers, inflated pods. The supplier's page is reported to say “Native to South America”, which conflicts with POWO.

images.alt: Cleome arborea in an air-pot on a wooden stool: hairy, purple-tinged stems carrying large palmate leaves of about seven leaflets

records.name: Farfugium japonicum (L.) Kitam.
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 2 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.note: Label is handwritten and partly buried in the photograph: “FARFUGIUM” and a second line beginning “TATSU…”. The leaves are crinkled, so this may be a named cultivar; not confirmed. Not technically an Australis plant; the bed has a space for some japonicums.
records.native_range: S. China to Temp. E. Asia
records.diagnostic: Spreading evergreen perennial to about 60 cm, with long-stalked, rounded, leathery, glossy dark green leaves like lily pads. Clusters of yellow daisy flowers are held above the foliage in autumn. Garden forms include spotted, variegated and crinkled-leaved cultivars.
records.work_done: Planted.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 3 Oct 2026. Acta Phytotax. Geobot. 8: 268 (1939). University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions.
records.open_questions: Read the full label and copy it word for word. Confirm whether it is a cultivar, such as ‘Crispatum’ or ‘Shishi Botan’. Diagnostic from a secondary source; check against the plant. Basionym Tussilago japonica L. (1767).

images.alt: A newly planted Farfugium japonicum with large, glossy, crinkled dark green leaves in bare soil, a white label in front of it

records.name: Fuchsia jimenezii Breedlove, P.E.Berry & P.H.Raven
records.det: T. Hart Dyke (verbal), relayed to D.C. Chambers, 2 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.label_read: “Fuchsia jimenezii £7.50 / Schufia type Fuchsia from central USA. Upright habit, deep glossy glabrous foliage and rose pink/ rose red small flowers. Very unusual! / Grown for Lullingstone World Garden”
records.note: Label: “central USA” should read Central America. The species sits in sect. Jimenezia, not sect. Schufia, though it is reported as closest to the Schufia lineage.
records.provenance: Plant-sale stock, “Grown for Lullingstone World Garden” (label). Grower not named.
records.diagnostic: Scrambling subshrub 0.5–1.5 m tall, entirely hairless. Leaves opposite, somewhat leathery, 5–11.5 cm long, flushed purple beneath. Many small rose-red to red flowers in terminal racemes through the year, with stamens bent back. Fruit a near-round red berry 10–12 mm across.
records.work_done: Planted.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 2 Oct 2026. Ann. Missouri Bot. Gard. 69: 221 (1982). IPNI (sect. Jimenezia); Fuchsietum; Wikipedia.
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. Protologue not read.

records.habit: Tuberous geophyte; seasonally dry tropical biome

records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check against the plant. T. Hart Dyke says this young plant is different from the established red Dahlia coccinea in the same bed, though both carry the same name; what it is is not yet known.

records.det: D.C. Chambers, 8 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.native_range: Europe to N. Iran, NW. Africa, Azores
records.diagnostic: Evergreen conifer with reddish-brown flaking bark. Needles flat, linear, 1–4 cm, dark green above and paler beneath, in two ranks on side shoots. Seeds held in a fleshy red aril. All parts except the aril flesh are highly poisonous.
records.work_done: Cut back, pruned and up-limbed.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 8 Oct 2026. Sp. Pl.: 1040 (1753).

records.name: Quercus robur L.
records.det: D.C. Chambers, 8 Oct 2026 — not keyed
records.common_names: Common oak, English oak, pedunculate oak
records.diagnostic: Deciduous tree. Leaves lobed, almost stalkless, with small ear-like lobes (auricles) at the base. Acorns on long stalks (peduncles). Sessile oak, Q. petraea, has stalked leaves without auricles and stalkless acorns.
records.work_done: Cut back, pruned and up-limbed.
records.sources: POWO, accessed 8 Oct 2026. Sp. Pl.: 996 (1753).
records.open_questions: Diagnostic from secondary sources; check leaf base and acorn stalks to rule out Q. petraea.
